hero.description: Climatica lets you explore the global WorldClim dataset interactively, through Walter–Lieth diagrams, climate charts and maps. Pick any point on land to see its climate normals or the weather of a single year, compare two places or two periods, or see on a map how the climate varies across a whole region. No account, nothing to install.

howItWorks.intro: Every value on screen takes the same path, from a global raster archive to your browser.

archive.label: Source
archive.title: WorldClim archive
archive.text: Global monthly rasters of temperature and precipitation: 30-year climate normals and yearly weather downscaled from CRU TS.

scrapi.label: Service
scrapi.title: SCRAPI
scrapi.text: An API from the {university} that answers questions about the rasters: the values of a cell, a box or a polygon, and the map tiles that draw a variable over a region.

climatica.label: Interface
climatica.title: Climatica
climatica.text: Asks SCRAPI for the cells you pick and draws them as diagrams, tables and maps, caching the answers so repeated questions are fast.

sources.intro: Climatica keeps no climate data of its own. The values, the place names and the maps come from these sources.

scrapi.text: SCRAPI is the API Climatica reads every value from. It publishes the WorldClim rasters as linked data and answers point, region and metadata queries.

privacy.account: No account is needed, and nothing identifies you.
privacy.storage: Your settings and recent places stay in this browser's storage, and your language in a cookie. Clearing the site's data resets them.
privacy.location: “Use my location” asks your browser for your position only when you press it, and sends only the coordinates, to fetch their data.

findPlace.intro: City Climate, Compare Cities and Compare Periods start from a place. There are four ways to pick one.

name.title: Search by name
name.text: Type a city or town in the search field and pick it from the list. Names work in many languages.

coordinates.title: Type coordinates
coordinates.text: Enter latitude and longitude, such as 46.4907, 11.3398, and choose “Go to coordinates”. The label names the nearest settlement.

map.title: Click the map
map.text: Click anywhere on land. The data are for that exact point; the label names the nearest settlement.

location.title: Use my location
location.text: Your browser's position, if you allow it. The data are for where you are; the label names the nearest settlement.

walterLieth.intro: A Walter–Lieth diagram shows a place's year at a glance: the temperature and precipitation curves, and the areas between them that tell humid months from arid ones.
walterLieth.scale: Both curves share one axis at a fixed scale, 1 °C to {ratio} mm, so a month whose precipitation curve falls below the temperature curve is arid. Above {breakpoint} mm, precipitation is compressed {compression} times so that very wet months still fit.

compare.cities: Two places side by side, for the same period or year: the stats table, both diagrams and the difference between them.
compare.periods: One place across climate normals or weather years, to see how its climate has changed.

layouts.split: Side by side: each series in its own panel. Expand one across the card when you need detail.
layouts.overlay: Overlay: the series in one diagram, told apart by their marker shapes, with one of them shaded.

filters.sidebar: The filters (dataset, period or year, variables, resolution and months) are in the sidebar on wide screens and behind the Filters chip on phones. Change them, then press “{apply}”.
filters.autoApply: In <link>Settings</link> you can turn auto-apply on or off: when it is on, filters apply as you change them; when it is off, they wait for “{apply}”. You can also keep the place and the filters in step across pages.

export.intro: The export menu above each chart saves what you see:
export.share: Every page keeps its place, filters and view in the address, so copying the URL shares exactly that view. Exported images carry the link too.

resolution.question: Why do the values change when I change the resolution?
resolution.answer: Each value describes the whole grid cell around your point, and a coarser cell covers more ground, often different elevations and landscapes. A change is expected. <link>See how the resolutions differ</link>.

elevation.question: Why does the elevation differ from the place's official elevation?
elevation.answer: It's the mean elevation of the grid cell, not that of a town centre or a weather station. In valleys and on slopes, a cell can be hundreds of metres higher or lower than the town; a finer resolution comes closer.

thirtySeconds.question: Why isn't {finest} available for every period?
thirtySeconds.answer: WorldClim publishes {finest} rasters only for its {period} climate normals. SCRAPI computes the other normals from WorldClim's yearly weather data, which goes down to {fallback}, so those periods do too.

cell.whole: Every value Climatica shows belongs to the raster cell that contains your point, not to the point itself. The map outlines that cell.
cell.mixed: A coarse cell can take in a valley floor and the slopes above it, or a coast and the land behind it. Its value is the average of all of them, so it may not match any one spot exactly.
cell.example: Bolzano ({period} normal) is a good example. The town sits on the floor of an Alpine valley, at about {valleyElevation} m. At {coarseGrid} its cell covers the surrounding mountains as well as the valley floor, so the cell's mean elevation is {coarseElevation} m and its mean annual temperature {coarseTemperature} °C. At {fineGrid} the cell covers only the valley floor: {fineElevation} m and {fineTemperature} °C, much closer to the town itself.
cell.illustrationLabel: Schematic of two cells containing the same point. {coarse}: the large cell, among its neighbours. {fine}: the small cell inside it, holding the point.
cell.illustrationCaption: Cells containing the same point at two resolutions (schematic, sizes at the equator).
cell.calloutTitle: Values change with the resolution — this is expected.
cell.calloutText: Each period opens at the finest resolution available for it. Choose a coarser resolution to see the average over a larger area.

resolutions.intro: WorldClim's grids are measured in arc-minutes and arc-seconds. A cell is roughly square at the equator and narrows towards the poles.
resolutions.caption: Spatial resolutions, their cell sizes and availability
resolutions.everywhere: Every climate normal and weather year

periods.averaged: averaged from the yearly weather data
periods.weatherIntro: Each year's monthly values, {first}–{last}: CRU TS downscaled by WorldClim.

indicators.intro: Climatica computes three indicators from the monthly values. T is a month's mean temperature (the average of its maximum and minimum), P its precipitation.

arid.title: Arid month
arid.text: Precipitation below twice the mean temperature: the precipitation curve under the temperature curve in a Walter–Lieth diagram. A month exactly at P = 2T counts as humid.

frost.title: Frost month
frost.text: A mean minimum temperature below 0 °C, marked by the frost band under the diagram.

martonne.title: De Martonne aridity index
martonne.text: Annual precipitation (mm) divided by the annual mean temperature plus 10 °C; lower is drier. It isn't defined where the annual mean temperature is −10 °C or lower.

figure.aridBar: An arid month: its precipitation bar is drawn in the arid colour, because precipitation is below twice the mean temperature (P < 2T).
figure.frostLine: A frost month: the minimum temperature line runs below 0 °C.
figure.aridCount: Arid months: how many months of the year are arid.
figure.martonne: The De Martonne aridity index for the year, with its class.
